Unless our democracy and governance is defined by something greater than 'everyone gets a chance to vote and they won't always be happy with the outcome' O'Toole's reasoning is fundamentally flawed.

Our parliament should be representative of the wishes of the people who elected it, and we are no where near that.

In the last election 39.5% of those who voted voted Liberal, that party now holds 54% of the seats - how is that, in any reasonable discussion, reflective of how people voted?

Answer: It is not.

Yes, democracies will always have a certain level of frustration attached to the electoral process - everybody cannot win - but to say that "The electoral reform process plays on frustration by suggesting that political nirvana lies just over the next hill" is disingenuous. Those of us who want electoral reform (and regardless of what some may say we are the majority) are not seeking nirvana, we are seeking a parliament that is representative of how the nation voted.

O'Toole says

PR advocates claim that proportionality helps make "votes count" because it ensures the seat count in the House of Commons better reflects the popular vote. This is inherently condescending, as it suggests that your vote doesn't count unless it elects an MP.

It is not condescending, it is a simple statement of fact. One person on the ballot takes a seat in the House of Commons, and quite frankly they are far more interested in toeing the line their leader sets than with what matters to the [likely] majority of voters in the riding who cast a vote for some other candidate.

Of that, O'Toole says

Most MPs are already elected with or near the 50% mark,

Really?

I went to the elections Canada website and took the results from the last election for the 1st ten ridings listed - three of them have MP's elected with 50% or more of the vote. If anyone wants to go through the list on a riding by riding basis and dispute me then go for it, but at this point I'm calling O'Toole's statement b/s something that he wants to believe instead of what actually happens.
